title: Repair a frost-cracked barrel, bucket or tote
summary: Ice splits plastic barrels, buckets and totes. HDPE and polypropylene can be welded with a heat gun and a strip of the same plastic, or a cut-out crack can be bolted over with a patch and a gasket; glue barely sticks to them. Use only food-safe materials on a container for drinking water, and drain it or leave room for ice next winter.

materials.item: Heat gun or hot-air plastic welder, with a narrow or speed-weld tip
Filler strips cut from an offcut of the same plastic (same resin code), thicker than milk-jug plastic
Drill bit about 5 mm (3/16 in) for stop holes
Patch plate of the same plastic, bigger than the hole all round
Gasket rubber listed for drinking water (NSF/ANSI 61), or cut from a food-grade seal
Bolts, nuts and wide washers that won't rust (stainless)
Bulkhead tank fitting and plug, for a round hole
Warm soapy water, a scraper and coarse sandpaper
Marker or paint to label containers NOT FOR DRINKING

steps.text: Empty the container and find out what it held. Don't use a container that held toxic chemicals such as bleach or pesticides for drinking water (CDC water supply).
steps.warn: Never heat, cut or weld a container that held fuel, oil or solvents: vapour inside can explode ([hot work on containers](#guides/safety_hot_work_containers)).

steps.text: Read the resin code moulded into the bottom: 2 is HDPE, 4 is LDPE, 5 is polypropylene (Sioux Falls RIC). These soften with heat and can be welded with a strip of the same plastic; thermosets don't soften and can't be welded (Master Appliance welding).
Find both ends of every crack in good light, flexing the wall gently. Drill a stop hole about 5 mm (3/16 in) at each end so the crack can't run further (Practical Sailor tanks, Permatex tank kit).
steps.warn: Clamp small containers and keep your hand out of the drill's path.

steps.text: Wash the area with warm soapy water and dry it (Master Appliance welding). Sand round the crack to fresh plastic; Permatex's tank kit asks for at least 2.5 cm (1 in) beyond the damage.
Cut a V-groove along the crack with a knife or file, so the filler has somewhere to go (Master Appliance welding).

Cut filler strips from an offcut of the same plastic, ideally the same container. Only like plastics fuse: PP rod on PP, PE on PE (Master Appliance welding). Thicker strips are easier: thin milk-jug strips tend to fall into the crack (Practical Sailor tanks).
Practise on a scrap first. The heat is right when the strip goes soft and tacky; if it turns liquid, it's too hot (Master Appliance welding).
steps.warn: Heat guns and molten plastic burn; a Master Appliance gun reaches 650 °C (1,200 °F). Work outdoors or with a window open and keep your head out of the fumes: TWI says polypropylene fumes aren't normally a worry except in a confined space with poor airflow (TWI fumes). Stop if plastic smokes.

steps.text: Heat the groove until its surface softens, then feed the strip into it in a steady line, pressing it down rather than pulling it. You want a small bead of soft plastic moving ahead of the strip; if the surface starts to burn, move faster (Master Appliance welding). Weld over the stop holes too.

Let it cool to room temperature before you test it (Master Appliance welding). Thick walls may need a second pass (Master Appliance welding), but repeated heating can widen the crack, so don't overdo it (Practical Sailor tanks).

For a hole or a crack you can't weld, cut the damage out to a smooth round or oval hole with no sharp corners (Poly Processing repair). Poly Processing says tanks already in the field are most often repaired by sealing such a hole with a blind fitting, plug or similar part (Poly Processing repair). At home that means a bulkhead tank fitting and plug, or a bolted patch of the same plastic with a gasket under it and a plate or wide washers inside; the paper does not describe that patch, so treat it as a stop-gap.
steps.warn: A cut with a corner or a notch starts a new crack; file every edge round and smooth.

steps.text: Fill it with water where it will stand, on a dry surface, and leave it for an hour or more to watch for leaks. Water weighs 1 kg a litre, so a full 200 L barrel is about 200 kg: don't try to move it full.

Before it holds drinking water, wash it with soap and rinse the soap out completely: bleach mixed with ammonia, vinegar or other acids, or other cleaners gives off toxic gas ([chemical hazards](#browse/hazards/chemical)). Then mix 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of unscented liquid bleach (5–9 % sodium hypochlorite) into 1 quart (about 1 litre) of water and use it to wet every inside surface; for a big barrel, mix more at the same strength or wipe it on. Wait at least 30 seconds, pour it out and let it air-dry (CDC water supply).
If the repair used glue, epoxy, a resin kit or any part you can't show is food-safe, mark the container NOT FOR DRINKING and use it for washing, flushing or the garden.

Before the next freeze, drain it or bring it indoors. Store an empty barrel upside down or on its side so rain and snow can't collect (ABCA rain barrels). See [water in winter](#guides/skill_water_in_winter).

notes:
## Why it cracked
Ice is about 9 % less dense than water (USGS water density), so freezing water needs more room than it had. In a full container with no room, the ice pushes the walls apart. Even a little water left in a rain barrel can crack it (ABCA rain barrels).

## Know your plastic
| Code | Plastic | Weld it? | Found as |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | HDPE | Yes, with HDPE strip | Milk and juice jugs, other packaging (Sioux Falls RIC) |
| 4 | LDPE | Yes, with LDPE strip | Dispensing and wash bottles, tubing, bags (Sioux Falls RIC) |
| 5 | PP | Yes, with PP strip | Moulded parts, pipe, rope (Sioux Falls RIC) |
| None | Cross-linked PE | No, not by ordinary welding | Some rotomoulded tanks (Poly Processing repair) |
| None | Thermosets | No: they don't soften with heat | (Master Appliance welding) |

The makers of welding kits say to identify the plastic so you use the right rod, and that only like plastics fuse (Master Appliance welding). Go by the code moulded into the container, not by how it looks or feels. PVC (code 3) gives off hydrochloric acid when it burns (Sioux Falls RIC): don't torch or overheat it.

## Why glue won't hold
Polyethylene has very low surface energy: glues can't wet it, and it has no pores for them to grip. Bonds across a crack are weak and won't take the load of a full tank (Poly Processing repair). Practical Sailor's long-term tests had only limited success with epoxy and polyurethane on polyethylene tanks (Practical Sailor tanks). Glues sold for plastic tanks are for small damage: one common kit is limited to cracks up to 10 cm (4 in) and holes up to about 1 cm (3/8 in), (Permatex tank kit). Don't assume any glue or resin is safe for drinking water: look for the maker saying so, or an NSF/ANSI 61 listing.

## Welding: what to expect
Hot-air welding melts the surface and a filler strip of the same plastic so they fuse (Poly Processing repair). The heat leaves stresses in the plastic as it cools, and uses up the stabilisers that protect it, so the welded area ends up weaker than the rest (Poly Processing repair). So keep a welded container for jobs where a leak costs little: on the ground, not up on a stand. Practical Sailor notes that tank makers don't recommend these repairs. Its own long-term tests of repairs reinforced with stainless-steel mesh looked promising, but it says the result is not a true fusion weld, that melting the plastic all the way makes it shrink away from the crack, and that the repeated heating needed can widen the crack (Practical Sailor tanks).

The four rules from a welding kit maker: like plastic on like, the right temperature with the work pre-heated, even pressure on the rod, and a steady speed (Master Appliance welding).

## Bolted patches
On tanks already in use, mechanical repair is the most common fix, for both ordinary and cross-linked polyethylene. The damage is cut out to a round or oval hole and closed with a plug, a blind fitting or a similar part that covers it. The cut must be smooth with no sharp corners: a notch concentrates stress, and ordinary polyethylene can crack right across from it as the tank is filled and emptied (Poly Processing repair).

## Food-safe only, for drinking water
- The CDC says it is best to store drinking water in FDA-approved food-grade containers, which don't pass toxic substances into the water, and not in containers that held toxic chemicals such as bleach or pesticides (CDC water supply).
- Every part touching the water counts: the patch, the gasket, the sealant. The standard for parts that touch drinking water, NSF/ANSI/CAN 61, covers gaskets, sealants, coatings, pipe and fittings, and checks what chemicals leach out of them into the water (UL NSF 61). Look for NSF/ANSI 61 (or NSF 61) on salvaged gaskets and fittings. In Canada the Standards Council of Canada accredits several certifiers for it, among them CSA, NSF, UL, IAPMO and BNQ (Health Canada products and materials).
- A strip from the same food-grade container is the safest filler, because it is the same plastic.
- If you don't know, label it NOT FOR DRINKING. Washing, toilet-flushing and garden water need containers too.

## Next winter
- Drain barrels and totes before the first freeze. Rinse them, take off the hoses and tap and store them inside the barrel, and keep the barrel in a basement, garage or under a deck, or turn it upside down or on its side outdoors (ABCA rain barrels).
- Water you must keep where it can freeze needs room to grow: never fill a rigid container to the brim: ice takes up roughly a tenth more room than the water it came from (USGS gives a 9 % drop in density; the sum is ours). Room helps but is no promise, since even a little water can crack a barrel as it freezes (ABCA rain barrels).
- The CDC says to keep stored drinking water cool, at 10–21 °C (50–70 °F), out of direct sun and away from fuel and pesticides, and to replace it every six months (CDC water supply). See [water in winter](#guides/skill_water_in_winter).

## When to leave it
A container that is brittle all over (it cracks again when flexed, or is chalky from years of sun), one that held fuel, solvents or pesticides, and one with a crack longer than you can weld in one sitting. Downgrade it to non-drinking use, or cut it up for patches, scoops and funnels.
